passage:
Subject: please read when you're alone

Shalini Didi,
I told Amma and Appa last week that I got the campus offer from the logistics company. I didn't. I didn't even clear the second round. And the backlogs from third semester are still there; I've been saying they're cleared since June.
Every Sunday call, Appa asks about joining dates, and I invent another detail. I've started dreading the phone. Yesterday Amma told the whole family group about "Kamal's job", and I sat on my hostel bed feeling sick.
I can't keep this going till July. I'm more scared of their faces than of anything else. Can you be on the call with me this Sunday when I tell them? I'll say it myself. I just don't want to be alone for it.
Kamal

qa.q: What did Kamal tell Amma and Appa last week?
qa.a: Kamal told them about getting the campus offer from the logistics company.

qa.q: What is Kamal most afraid of?
qa.a: Kamal is most scared of seeing the parents' disappointment, which shows in dreading the phone and feeling sick after the family group message.

qa.q: Which step in the email is a wise one, and why?
qa.a: Asking Shalini Didi to be on the call while Kamal tells the truth is wise, because support makes it easier to stop the lies before July.

qa.q: What might it be like for Amma and Appa to hear the truth on Sunday?
qa.a: They may feel shocked and disappointed, especially after telling the family, but hearing it from Kamal now is better than finding out later.

grounding: A student who claimed a job offer while failing admits to Shalini Didi how fear of disappointing the parents has turned the story into a trap.

passage:
My first year of pharmacy college? A performance, honestly. I'm Minakshi, and I failed two papers in the first semester. On the phone I told my parents I'd scored eighty-five percent. My father handed out sweets at his shop for "our topper daughter". After that I couldn't take it back.
In the second semester I had to keep inventing: a certificate that was "still being printed", a professor who had "praised me in class". I stopped going home for festivals, because I couldn't look at the sweets box.
It ended when the college posted the result sheet home. My mother called, very quiet, and asked, "Why didn't you trust us?" I cried for an hour. We're still repairing it. The failing was fixable. The story nearly wasn't.

qa.q: What score did Minakshi tell her parents she had?
qa.a: Minakshi told them she'd scored eighty-five percent.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel she couldn't take the lie back?
qa.a: Her father had already handed out sweets at his shop, so she felt ashamed and afraid of disappointing him in front of everyone.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: Each lie needed another until the result sheet exposed it; telling her parents after the first semester, perhaps with a college counsellor's support, would have kept it fixable.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's mother have felt when she asked, "Why didn't you trust us?"
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and sad that her daughter couldn't tell her the truth, more than angry about the failed papers.

grounding: A young woman tells how hiding failed papers from a proud family turned into a trap that grew worse than the failure itself.

passage:
The paddy was nearly cut, and the whole village near Champhai had come to help Lalremsiami's family bring in the harvest. Lalremsiami's father told everyone at the tea break, "My daughter has passed all her nursing papers. First class!"
Lalremsiami smiled and handed around the cups. She had failed two papers in the last semester. She had written "passed" in her messages home, and it had seemed easier than hearing her father go quiet on the phone.
That evening her college friend Sarita called. "The re-exam form closes on Friday. Did you fill it?"
"Not yet."
"Siami, you have to. And your family?"
"They think I passed."
Sarita was silent a moment. "Every week it gets bigger."
Lalremsiami looked out at her father laughing by the fire. She felt the trap close a little more.

qa.q: How many papers had Lalremsiami failed?
qa.a: She had failed two papers in the last semester.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she looked at her father laughing by the fire?
qa.a: She felt trapped and guilty, afraid of disappointing him yet aware that each week the false story grew.

qa.q: What would you advise Lalremsiami to do next?
qa.a: Fill in the re-exam form before Friday and tell her family the truth soon, perhaps with a trusted relative or Sarita's support.

qa.q: How does Sarita see the situation?
qa.a: Sarita sees the lie growing every week and worries about her friend, which is why she reminds her about the form and the family.

grounding: It shows a student in a proud family claiming to have passed while quietly failing, and the gap between story and reality becoming a trap.

passage:
On Sunday video calls, Javier's parents in Valencia always asked about the internship. "It's going well," he said every week, sitting in front of the same bookshelf in his Madrid room. There was no internship. He had failed two exams in January and spent the spring retaking them.
His flatmate Amara sometimes heard the calls through the thin wall. One evening she knocked. "Your mum just told my mum on the group chat that they're flying up for your 'end of internship' dinner."
Javier's face went grey. "When?"
"The fifteenth."
He sat on the bed. "I didn't want them to think they wasted all that money on me."
Amara sat beside him. "They'll be more hurt that you carried this alone. Call them tonight. I'll stay in the kitchen if you want someone nearby."
He picked up his phone.

qa.q: Where do Javier's parents live?
qa.a: They live in Valencia.

qa.q: How did Javier feel when Amara told him about the dinner?
qa.a: He felt panicked and ashamed, his face going grey, because the false story he told to avoid disappointing his parents was about to collapse.

qa.q: What could fix the situation, as Amara suggests?
qa.a: Calling his parents that night and telling them the truth, with Amara nearby, before the trip makes it bigger.

qa.q: How might Javier's parents feel if they arrived for a dinner that isn't real?
qa.a: They would likely feel shocked and hurt, more by being kept in the dark than by the failed exams.

grounding: It shows a student hiding failure from parents with a false internship story until the gap between story and reality becomes a trap.

passage:
In the college hostel common room, Kishore's phone lit up: "Amma calling." He stepped into the corridor.
"Beta, did the company confirm your joining date? Appa has told the whole family."
"Next week, Amma. They're finalising." There was no company. He had failed three papers and hadn't sat for placements at all.
He hung up and leaned against the wall. The story had started small in January, one "I did fine" after an exam. Now there was a job, a salary, a city. Every call needed more details.
Rehana, the final-year student who ran the peer support desk, stopped beside him. "You okay? You look like you're going to be sick."
Kishore laughed weakly. Then, to his own surprise, he told her everything.
"That's a heavy thing to carry alone," Rehana said. "The counsellor is in till five. Want me to walk you there?"
He nodded.

qa.q: How many papers had Kishore failed?
qa.a: Three papers.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he leaned against the wall?
qa.a: Kishore felt trapped and sick with dread, as the small January lie had grown into a job, a salary and a city.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed he looked unwell, listened, named it as heavy to carry alone, and offered to walk him to the counsellor right away.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa feel if the truth comes out later rather than now?
qa.a: They would likely feel shocked and hurt, especially after Appa told the whole family, and the longer it goes on the harder it gets.

grounding: Shows a student in a high-expectation family claiming a job while failing, and the gap between story and reality becoming a trap.
